questions.question: State the purpose of a design presentation, identify the three audiences in the room and what each needs, and name the three qualities that earn an audience's trust.
questions.expected_answer: The purpose is to let people who did not do the work understand the problem, judge the evidence and decide whether the solution deserves support; it is the portfolio spoken aloud in order with the model in hand, not a display of effort or a sales pitch. The assessor needs each step of the design process named and evidenced; the class needs to learn what was tried and what happened, including failures; the client, such as a stall owner, needs cost, what would change for them and reasons to trust the solution. Trust is earned by evidence such as counts, photographs and measured results, by specificity such as exact costs and loads rather than vague words, and by candour in stating failed tests and the fixes before being asked.

questions.question: Set out a five-minute presentation structured around the design process, giving the content and approximate timing of each part and explaining how speakers are allocated.
questions.expected_answer: About thirty seconds opens with the problem told as a story from the investigation with one number and one photograph; forty-five seconds gives the brief in problem form and the key specifications with their reasons; sixty seconds shows both sketches and explains the comparison and choice; forty-five seconds points to the isometric drawing and development, hands the model to the audience and describes what changed in the making and why, with a photograph; ninety seconds presents the evaluation, passes briefly, fails fully with causes and recommendations, then returns to the brief with the estimated reduction in harm, the benefit kept and the solution's own footprint; thirty seconds closes with numbered recommendations and an invitation for questions. Every member speaks, with each presenting the part they did first-hand, planned handovers, and notes on cards rather than read pages.

questions.question: Explain how the model, drawings and tables are used during the presentation, the rules for delivery and rehearsal, and how questions should be answered.
questions.expected_answer: The model is held up at the start, passed round during the making section and held again during the evaluation so results are shown on the object; drawings are pointed to and named rather than described; tables are shown large with at most seven rows and fails highlighted, alongside two or three photographs, and text-heavy slides are avoided. Speakers stand clear of the visuals, speak to the back row at conversational pace, pause at handovers, hold the model steady and look at the audience; the presentation is rehearsed twice with a timer, once before another team that asks questions, and cut to time so the evaluation is not lost. Questions are heard in full, repeated briefly, answered directly with evidence by the member who did that part; if the answer is unknown the team says so and explains how it would find out, never arguing, guessing numbers or letting one member answer everything.
